Murad Reza, Addl. AG with Md Al Amin Sarkar; DAG -----For Respondent No. 4.

Vs.
Bangladesh Power Development Board and others ------ Respondents
full_judgment:
Md Khurshid Alam Sarkar J: This Rule was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the impugned decision taken by respondent Nos. 1 and 4 upon showing the petitioner's financial proposal to be non-responsive in relation to the tender under reference No. 2781- BPDB (Sets)/Dev-205/2011 for engineering, design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ± 10% Power Plant (HFO fired Engine Generating Sets.) Project on turnkey basis in Amnura, Chapainawabganj, Bangladesh, shall not be declared to have been taken without lawful authority and of no legal effect and, further, to show. cause as to why respondent Nos. 1 and 4 shall not be directed to declare that the petitioner's financial proposal is responsive as well as the lowest and thereby to award the tender under reference No. 2781/2011 BPDB (Shct.)/Dev-205/2011 in favour of the petitioner as the same is technically responsive and financially the lowest and/or pass such other or further order or orders as to this Court may seem fit and proper.

2. The facts of the case, as stated in the writ petition, are that the petitioner being incorporated as a company in the year 1982 engaged itself in carrying out engineering, construction and various large scale development programs in Highway, Bridge, and Building including the land mark construction and maintenance of Dhaka- Chittagong Highway, Dhaka-Sylhet Highway, Highways of Dinajpur, Rangpur, Rajshahi and Khulna, 300fts wide Purbachal link road and, eventually, the petitioner diversified its business from infrastructure to Power Generation from 2007 and pursued several powers projects. When respondent No. 1 invited tender on 9-10-2011 for engineering design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ±10% Power Plant (HFO fired Engine Generating Sets.) project on turnkey basis at Amnura, Chapai-nawabganj, Bangladesh, the petitioner participated in the said tender by submitting the 'Technical Proposal' to which the commitment letter from the financier was appended and the 'Financial Proposal' as per the procedure prescribed in the tender document. On 25-6-2012 the respondents opened the Technical Proposals and found 5 bidders, including the petitioner company, to be technically responsive and, then, respondent No. 2 vide letter dated 14-10-2012 notified the petitioner that their 'Financial Proposal' would be opened on 2I -10-2012 at 11 am local time in respondent No. 1,s Board room. After opening up the 'Financial Proposal' of the technically responsive 5 bidders, there were communications from Hardy Capital Corporation, which is the financier of the petitioner company. On 3-12-2012 to respondent No.1 in order to provide a reassurance of funding the project and vide letter dated 17-12- 2012 the said financier company provided certain clarifications to respondent No. 1 in relation to the anomalies as to the letterhead and logo of their company. It is stated that though the bidders were notified that the 'Financial Offer' would be opened on 21-10-2012 but nothing was notified to any of the bidders as to their financial offers. It is alleged that the respondents failed to show any transparency in dealing with the said tender and making the bidders financially responsive or non- responsive given that from the date of finding the petitioner to be technically responsive, there was no communication between the petitioner and the respondents. When on 25.02.2013 'The Daily Star', a leading daily newspaper of the land, published news under the title "Harbin Deal Gets Government Nod Again", only then the petitioner had the opportunity to know that the Purchase Committee approved the aforementioned project in favour of the China Company Hubei Electric Power Survey and Design i.e. respondent No.5 for a price of Taka 948 crores. The petitioner then managed to obtain a copy of the summary of the purchase proposal, which was prepared on the basis of the evaluation report of the Tender Evaluation Committee (hereinafter referred to TEC), wherein the TEC considered the financial proposal of all the 5 technical responsive bidders and found the petitioner's financial proposal to be non-responsive.

3. It is alleged that the petitioner offered Taka 200 crores less than that of respondent No.5 who was recommended the award but on the ground of lacking some frivolous and petty requirements the petitioner was made financially non-responsive just to favour respondent No. 5 purposefully and the action of respondent Nos. 1 & 2 in offering the tender to respondent No. 5 demonstrates mala fides as the petitioner has been deprived of getting the award for the personal gain of the respondents and against the financial interest of the State at the cost of huge loss of Bangladesh. The petitioner on 27-12-2012 notified respondent Nos. 1 &2 about the action of respondent No. 4 when the latter explained its position to the former stating that the petitioner's financial proposal was not found responsive for the reasons stated in the minutes of the meeting of TEC on 8-1-2013. It is stated that since the petitioner was not supplied with any decision, she was not in a position to prefer an appeal to the appellate authority and under the circumstances the petitioner was compelled to approach this Court for vindication of her legal rights. By filing a supplementary affidavit on 06-10-2013, the petitioner stated that though this Hon'ble Court issued Rule on 10-3-2003 with a verbal direction upon the respondents to maintain statusquo, respondent Nos. 1-3 issued Notice of Award in favour of respondent No.5 on 14-3-2013 and the same was accepted by the latter on 18-3-2013 and, thereafter, on 31-3-2013 they sealed the agreement. The petitioner terms the aforesaid actions of the respondents to have been taken in sheer disregard of this Court's honour and practice.

4. Bangladesh Power Development Board (BPDB) is respondent No. 1, the Secretary of Bangladesh Power Development Board is respondent No.2, the Tender Evaluation Committee (TEC) of Bangladesh Power Development Board is respondent No.3, the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh represented by the Ministry of Power, Energy and Mineral Recourses Division is respondent No. 4 and HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute of China is respondent No.5 in this writ petition. Respondent Nos. 1-3 have entered their appearances and contested the case by a filing an affidavit-in-opposition followed by supplementary thereto and respondent No.4, though did not file any separate affidavit-in-opposition, adopted the statements and submissions of respondent Nos. 1-3. Respondent No.5 contested the Rule by filing a separate set of affidavit-in-opposition with a supplementary thereto.

5. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent Nos. 1-3, it is stated that BPDB invited Tender under 'Single-Stage Two-envelop Tendering Method' for engineering, design, manufacturing, inspection, supply, installation, erection, testing & commissioning of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW ±10% Power plant (HFO fired Engine Generating sets project on turnkey basis including 2 years warranty period along with LTSA for next 4 (four) years under the heading of "Construction of Chapai Nawabganj 100 MW. ± 1 0% Power plant (HFO fired Engine Generating sets) project "on 9-10-2011 vide Tender Ref. No. 2781-BPDB (Sect)/Dev-2051 2011 dated 9-10-2011. The said Tender Notice was published in several daily newspapers on 10- 10-2011, 13-10-2011 and 15-10-2011.

6. As per the Tender Notice and subsequent addenda, the Technical and Financial proposals, separated in two sealed envelopes, were to be submitted to BPDB by 10-00 hrs. BST on 25-6-2012. The Tender opening committee headed by the Secretary of BPDB was to open the Technical proposal at the same date and read out the names of the Tenders. The following 5(five) tenderers namely, 1.M/s.CCC:ETERN-FUJIAN JV (CFFJV), China, 2. M/s. HUBAI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China, 3. M/s. Energypac Power Generation Ltd. Bangladesh, 4. M/s. Concord Pragatee Construction Ltd, Bangladesh and 5.M/s.Dong Fang Electric International Corporation, China were received. All the Tenderers' representatives were present. As per clause 25 of the Tender documents, the Technical proposals submitted by the bidders were to be evaluated first and then the "Financial Proposals" of the Tenderers whose "Technical Proposals" found to be responsive would be opened and to be evaluated only. The technical proposals were evaluated by the TEC which was formed by the Power Division, Ministry of Power Energy and Mineral Resources and the said Committee recommended all the said tenderers as technically responsive after receiving requisite clarifications from them and, accordingly, further recommended to open their Financial Proposals which were finally approved by the BPDB and the concerned Ministry (MEMR).

7. Then the Financial Proposals of all the technically responsive tenderers were opened on 21-10-2012 and the evaluation of the financial proposals was done as per the instructions set forth in the tender document and subsequent addenda. As per the assessment of the TEC, only 2 (two) tenderers' financial proposals were found to be responsive namely: (1) M/s. CCC:ETERN- FUJIAN JV(CFFJV), China and (2) M/s. HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China and the following tenderers' Financial proposals were found to be non-responsive- (1) M/s. Energy Pac Power Generation Ltd. Bangladesh, (2) M/s. Concord Pragatee Construction Ltd, Bangladesh and (3) M/s. Dong Fang Electric International Corporation, China. The Financial proposal of M/s. Concord Pragatee Consortium Ltd. Bangladesh (the petitioner) was found non- responsive since her offer was confusing and conditional which falls under material deviation and the said decision was communicated to the petitioner vide memo No. 27/BPDB(Secy.) /Dev- 205/2011 and dated 3-1-2013. As the financial proposals of the petitioner and two other tenderers were found non-responsive, the same were not considered for further evaluation. The specific reasons for non-considering the writ petitioner's financial offer is given in the minutes of the meeting of TEC held on January 2013 (annexure-I to the writ petition).

8. The financial proposals of 2 responsive tenderers were evaluated by the TEC and after threadbare discussions and considering the facts and factors the said Committee recommended to accept the financial offer (EPC cost) of technically and financially responsive 1st Lowest Bid of M/s. HUBEI Electric Power Survey and Design Institute, China, (respondent No.5) which was subsequently recommended by BPDB and then was approved by the Purchase Committee and, finally, was received nod from the Hon'ble Prime Minister of the Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh. Thereafter, on 14-3-3013 the Notification of Award was issued in favour of respondent No.5 who accepted the same on 18-3- 2013 and submitted performance Guarantee (PG) on 28-3-2013 and thereafter a contract was signed between the BPDB and respondent No.5 on 31-3- 2013.

9. Out of 3 financially non-responsive tenderers, one M/s. Dong Fang Electric International Corporation went to the Review Panel invoking the provisions under sections 29 and 30 of the Public Procurement Act-2006 (PPA, 2006) and Public Procurement Rules-2008 (PPR, 2008) to seek redress for their grievance and after hearing both the sides the Review Panel rejected the said appeal on 10-2-2013. However, the writ petitioner, without exhausting the said provisions of law for settlement of her grievance, filed the instant writ petition and obtained the present Rule. It is started that as per clause 2. of the Tender Documents, Specimen Form of the Proposal (Form of Tender) 'without price' needed for technical proposal and Specimen Form of Tender 'with price' needed for financial proposal are furnished in Appendix-2 of the Tender Documents. As such, it cannot be said that the financial credit proposal of the writ petitioner has been evaluated with her technical proposal. It is further stated that when the writ petitioner's financial offer was found non-responsive she filed an application to respondent No.2 on 27-12-2012 and respondent No.2 after examining the matter rejected the said application of the writ petitioner on 3-1-2013 and, hence, it cannot be said that the writ petitioner was not informed about her financial offer as non- responsive.

10. In the affidavit-in-opposition filed by respondent No.5, it is contended that the claim of the petitioner as to making the lowest offer by a margin of Taka 200 crores appears to be based on the 'read-out' price as stipulated in the financial proposal of the submitted tender documents. It was mentioned by respondent No.5 that the readout price is not the final price to be accepted for determining the successful bidder. The technical and the financial proposal have to be evaluated and graded/scored in accordance with the provisions of the PPA, 2006 and PPR, 2008 having taken into consideration all the aspects of the technical proposal and the financial proposal. The 'present tender in question involves such method Of, procurement where the bidder will arrange finance for the tendered project and, therefore, in 'addition to read-out price, rate of interest, repayment period, arrangement' fees and other bank charge set should be taken into consideration for final evaluation of the financial proposal. Read- out price is actually the cost of Engineering, Procurement and, Construction Cost (EPC) and does' not include rate of interest, repayment period; arrangement fees and other charges and expenses as may be incurred. The petitioner, in his financial offer, has Claimed 5% as 'Lender Fee" culminating 4.25 million in Euro which is not included in the read-out price. Moreover, the read-out price of the petitioner also does not include USD 1,00,000 as commitment fees as referred to in their financial proposal. It is further stated that the petitioner- ranked 4th while respondent No.5 ranked 4th among all of the bidders (annexure-I series), All the process of tender was done lawfully, fairly and transparently.

11. Mr. Akhtar Imam, the learned advocate 'appearing for the petitioner, at the very outset, places sections 18& 60 of the PPA, 2006 and submits that the decision of respondent No.1 in finding' the petitioner's bid to be financially non- responsive has been made in sheer violation of the aforesaid provisions of the PPA, 2006 inasmuch as the same has been taken without seeking any clarification of the grounds taken by the TEC for showing the petitioner non-responsive and without communicating the result of the financial evaluation to the petitioner. In a bid to buttress up the, above submissions he adds that respondent No. 1 has, been provided with ample powers to seek clarifications and negotiate with the tenderers under sections 18 & 60 of the PPA, 2006 and by not seeking the clarifications from the petitioner in relation to the frivolous grounds shown to find the petitioner's offer to be financially non-responsive, the respondents have acted unlawfully in making the impugned decision and, as such, the respondents' decision must be termed as an offspring of their arbitrary and malafide action.

12. Mr. Akhtar refers to Clauses 17 & 25 of the Tender Documents and submits that respondent Nos. 1-4 grossly violated the instructions laid down in the tender documents in addition to the provisions of the PPA, 2006 inasmuch as the Tender Documents do not permit respondent Nos. 1-4 to examine the commitment letter at the financial evaluation stage and, further, the tender documents expressly state the procedure for financial evaluation which does not in any manner include considerations of material deviation, confusion and conditional commitment, rather Clauses 17 & 25 expressly made it clear that material deviation, confusion and conditional commitment are to be considered at the technical evaluation stage and, by referring to annexure-D&E to the writ petition, he submits that the same has already been done at the stage of technical evaluation when the petitioner was asked to clarify some issues raised by respondent Nos. 1-4 and upon receiving satisfactory clarifications the petitioner was declared technically responsive. He submits that commitment letter is part of the technical proposal and, hence, it was examined at the technical evaluation stage and the petitioner was found to be technically responsive. The contents of the letter dated 3-12-2012 is self-explanatory and nothing stated in the said letter can in any way be construed as an intention to influence the respondent Nos. 1-4. Moreover, the petitioner was found to be technically responsive on or before 21-10-2012 (the date of the financial opening) and, as such, the letter dated 3-12-2012 cannot influence a decision taken before 21-10-2012 and was totally redundant and of no legal consequence and should have been ignored. Thus, respondent Nos. 1-4 cannot legally declare the petitioner to be technically non-responsive at the financial evaluation stage after declaring the petitioner to be technically responsive at the technical evaluation stage, otherwise the respondents would be blamed for traveling beyond the powers provided in the Tender Documents.

13. He submits that the impugned decision has been taken having been influenced by the extraneous consideration in collusion with other respondents which is evident from the fact that though the petitioner was the lowest bidder with a margin of Taka 200 (two hundred) crores, respondent No.5 has been shown as the successful bidder causing a huge financial loss to Bangladesh. He submits that the decision making process of respondent Nos. 1-4 is flawed and reflects complete lack of transparency and, thus, this is a fit and appropriate case for this Court to exercise its judicial power of review in the light of the fact that respondent Nos. 1-4 demonstrated their arbitrariness very nakedly. Mr. Akhtar relies on the following decisions in support of his above sub- missions: Ramana vs I.A. Authority of India AIR 1979 (SC) 1628, M/S Kasturi Lal vs State of J&K AIR 1980 (SC) 1992, Ruhul Amin vs Freedom Fighters Welfare Trust 51 DLR 208, Agrogami Engineers Limited vs Bangladesh Bank 45 DLR 134, Hyundai Corporation vs Sumikin Bussan 54 DLR (AD) 88, Tata Cellular vs Union of India AIR 1996 (SC) 11, The Comptroller Auditor General vs KS Gallathan AIR 1987 (SC) 537, Harminder Singh vs Union of India AIR 1986 (SC) 1527, M/S Jyothi Krishna Engineers vs State Bank of Hyderabad AIR 1993 (AP) 327, Chowdhury Mahmud Hassan vs Bangladesh 54 DLR 537.

14. With regard to the issue of maintainability of this case, Mr. Akhter places Section 29(2)(c)(ii) and sections 18, 52 & 53 of the PPA, 2006 and submits that the petitioner could not exhaust the statutory remedy provided by the PPA, 2006 because the petitioner is required by the PPA, 2006 to file a claim prior to the approval of a bid by the Cabinet Purchase Committee and since the petitioner was not informed at any stage about the tender process and till date has not received a letter rejecting her bid, there was no alternative but to file the instant writ petition. He submits that the tender in the instant case is not an ordinary commercial contract since the terms of the contract must be in compliance with a statute namely PPA 2006 and the Rule framed thereunder namely, PPR 2008 in addition to be in consonance with Clause 33 of Instructions to Tender and must have the approval of the Cabinet Purchase Committee headed by the PM and, as such, the said contract is a statutory contract and, by placing the celebrated case of Sharping MSS Ltd vs Bangladesh 39 DLR (AD) 85, he submits that writ is always maintainable with regard to any grievance of a statutory contract. Finally, he submits that even if the contract was an ordinary commercial contract, writ petition is maintainable since the action complained of is blatantly arbitrary, discriminatory, malafide and violative of the fundamental rights of the petitioner guaranteed under Articles 27, 31 & 40 of the Constitution. In support of his submissions he refers to the following case laws: Abdul Rouf \IS Abdul Hamid 17 DLR (SC) (515 para 7), Khondoker Mostaque Ahmed vs Bangladesh 34 DLR (AD) 222 (para 17+23), Khandaker Ehteshamuddin Ahmed vs Bangladesh and others 33 DLR (AD) 154 (para 32), AFM Shah Alam vs Mujibul Haq, 41 DLR (AD) 68 (para 49 '3), Asaduzzaman vs Bangladesh.: 42 DLR (AD) 153 (para 3 'c), Kushtia Sugar Mills Ltd vs Chairman Labour Court, 49 DLR 237 (para 11). By making the aforesaid submissions the learned Advocate for the petitioner prays for making the Rule absolute.

15. Per contra, Mr Murad Reza, the learned Additional Attorney-General, appearing for the respondent No.4, at the very outset places Section 2(d) and section 7(1) of the Contract Act, 1872 and submits that an offer must be made by a party in the clearest terms and in an unambiguous manner and, thereafter, the acceptance to an offer must be absolute and unqualified. He refers to the letter dated 5-6-2012 issued by the petitioner's financial company (Hardy Capital Corp.) and submits that the petitioner's said financial by proposing to charge a commitment fees of 1,00,000 (USD) and a lending fee of 5% of the loan amount has, in fact, put a condition on the respondents. He further submits that the technical proposal of a bidder is to be evaluated according to the provisions of Section 59 of the PPA, 2006 and Rules 119-121 of the PPR, 2008. In an end eavour to elaborate his submissions on the provisions of the above Rule, he adds that as per Rules 120 & 121 of the PPR, 2008, the stipulated price/read out price as mentioned in the financial offer is not the only determinant for acceptance of a financial proposal and, thereafter, if the 'financial proposal of a bidder is the lowest offer, it does not entitle award of contract in view of the provisions of Rule 120 which provides that a financial proposal has to be evaluated in substance. Rules 120, 121(2) and 121(3) lay down formula as to how a financial proposal should be assessed when the evaluation of financial proposal has to be combined with the score obtained in the each respective technical proposal and thereby the most eligible bidder has to be selected. He submits that it is not either the technical proposal or the financial proposal alone that has to be taken into consideration for selecting the most eligible bidder. Therefore, the petitioner's prayer for awarding the tender in her favour is not tenable in law. The above provisions provide that assessment of eligibility on technical proposal is to be expressed in 'scoring'. As regards the technical proposal, the ranking indicates that the petitioner's technical offer was not on a par with that of respondent No. 5.

16. He refers to annexure-B and submits that the writ petitioner was rightly declared non-responsive with regard to her financial proposal as her papers and documents relating to financial proposal were found inconsistent and contrary to, the instructions laid down in the Tender Document. By placing Clause 17 of the Tender Documents he submits that in order to substantiate the source of finance of the each tenderer, a firm commitment letter from the financial lender about the tenderer's credit financing covering 100% of the turnkey price is required to be submitted with the technical proposal at the time of bid submission, otherwise the tender shall be considered technically non-responsive and, further, the tenderer shall enclose a complete and firm financing proposal. The Credit proposal shall mainly include (a) offered credit, (b) rate of interest, (c) repayment period, (d) grace period etc and the financial proposal should include 3 (three) amortization schedules considering above mentioned features of credit, 1 (one) for remaining portion of foreign currency, (except CIF value), 01 (one) for local currency and the BPDB will provide corporate guarantees against the credit financing.

17. Then, he places Clause 25 of the Tender Documents and by emphasizing on Sub-Clause 'b' of the part of "Material Deviation", he submits that the tender documents if submitted in deviation of the instructions laid down therein will be declared non-responsive. The financial proposal of the petitioner, he continues to submit, has not been prepared in line with Clause 17 and, therefore, it falls under stipulation regarding material deviation part of Clause 25 and was rightfully declared non-responsive. He submits that since the borrower is BPDB, the conditions stipulated in the petitioners' financial offer, in one hand, would create burden and limit in substantial way BPDB's negotiating capability, on the other hand, are inconsistent with, the tender document and, thereby, constitutes material deviations from the stipulations contained in the tender document and, accordingly, was rightly declared non-responsive.

18. Then he places sections 29 and 30 of the PPA, 2006 and Rules 56-60 of the PPR, 2008 and submits that the petitioner has not exhausted efficacious remedy available under law and, as such, the present writ petition is not maintainable. In a bid to elaborate his argument on this point he submits that for the sake of argument if it is conceded that the petitioner did not receive the annexure- 7 (communication by the respondents to the petitioner informing her that she was found non-responsive), however, since the petitioner was able to obtain a copy of the summary of the purchase proposal based on the Evaluation Report of the TEC, who considered the financial proposal of the respective parties and found the petitioner's financial proposal to be non-responsive, the petitioner could have easily invoked the statutory pro- visions as laid down in the PPA, 2006. He submits that it is an admitted fact that the petitioner vide letter dated 27-12-2012 to respondent No.4 elaborated her grievance in relation to the actions of the respondent Nos. 1 & 2 and thereafter instead of availing the forums available under the PPA, 2006 she opted to file the writ petition on 6-3- 2013 having wasted 2 months after lodging the said complaint. He submits under section 59 of the PPA, 2006 Review Panel is an equally efficacious forum as it has the power to pass any ad-interim order upon the respondents and in an endeavour to substantiate his argument he takes the instance of another bidder namely, Dongfang Electric International Corporation who filed com- plaint with the Procuring Entity on 26-12-2012, thereafter, with the Head of the Procuring Entity on'2-1-2013, thereafter, with the Secretary, Power Division on 10-1-2013 and, finally, the said company preferred the statutory appeal No. 3- 162/2013 before the Review Panel when the tender process was temporarily restrained. He submits that the writ petitioner's case does not fall under the exceptions as stipulated in section 29(2) of the PPA, 2006, as the petitioner was informed by respondent No. 2 about the grounds of non-responsiveness and her purported grievance clearly falls under Rule 56 (খ) (৯) of the PPR, 2008 since the tender in question is an open tender but the petitioner without seeking to avail of remedies as mentioned above filed this writ petition. He submits that under the provisions of Rules 59 & 60 of the PPR, 2008, the petitioner till now may avail the efficacious remedy before the Review Panel invoking Rule 56 (খ) (১২) of the PPR, 2008 which provides for grievance procedure to address complaints stemming from inappropriate conclusion of contract.

19. Mr. Murad Reza then refers to the case of Superintendent Engineer, RHD vs Md Eunus and Brothers (Pvt.) Ltd reported in 31BLD (AD) 1 and submits that the subject matter of the instant writ petition being pure and simple commercial con- tract, the present writ petition is not maintainable. Then, he refers to the case of Bangladesh Power Development Board vs Asaduzzaman Sikder; 9 BLC (AD) 1 and submits that the Apex Court in the said case held that writ jurisdiction can only be invoked if the contract is a statutory contract or if the Government enters into a contract in the sovereign capacity. Then, he refers to the case of Nuruddin vs Manager, Titas Gas Transmission and Distribution Company Ltd 18 BLD (AD) 273= 3 BLC (.4D) 231 and Shamsunnahar Salam vs Mohammad Wahidur Rahman, 51 DLR (AD) 231 and submits that since a question effect as to receiving the decision from the respondents on the tender application of the petitioner has been disputed, this Court cannot decide the said fact sit- ting in the capacity of certiorari. By referring to the case of State of Orissa vs Harinarayan AIR 1972 (SC) 1816, State of UP vs Vijay Bahadur Singh 1982 2 SCC 365, Union of India vs BW Ram AIR 1971 (SC) 2295, he submits that even if the petitioners financial offer would have been accepted provisionally by the respondents, the Government has the right to reject the same inasmuch as any bid accepted provisionally can be, rejected in the public interest by the government before issuance of Notification of Award.

20. Mr Razik Al Jalil, the learned advocate appearing for respondent Nos. 1-3, and Dr. Shahdeen Malik, the learned advocate appearing for respondent No.5, both of them opted to adopt the submissions advanced by Mr. Murad Reza. However, Dr. Malik, added a further submission that respondent Nos. 1-4 are government functionaries and in course of carrying out their routine tasks they have made a decision in favour of respondent No.5 in accordance with law and it is the settled principle of law that presumption on the decision made by a government functionary should be that the same has been taken bonafide unless any aggrieved person makes out a clear case of malafide by categorically stating the motive or dishonesty of the concerned government functionary. He submits that there is no specific allegation against the respondents in leveling blame against them that they have been influenced by extraneous consideration. By referring to the case of Farzana Haque vs University of Dhaka 42 DLR 262, he submits that malafide must be pleaded in clearer terms in a writ petition and requires to be proved by material evidence and, thus, malafide must not be readily inferred. By making the aforesaid submissions, the learned advocate for the respondents pray for discharging the Rule.

21. We have heard the learned advocates for both the sides, perused the writ petitions, affidavits-in-opposition together with their annexure, relevant laws and decisions placed before this Court which have been considered by us with great care.

22. The main contentious point in this case is that whether the decision made by the respondents as to finding the petitioner's bid financially non-responsive on the ground of lacking "Material Deviation" was made in compliance with the provisions of PPA, 2006, PPR, 2008 and the instructions stipulated in the Tender Document in the backdrop of declaring the petitioner technically responsive. The further issue falls for consideration by this Court is whether the writ petition is maintainable in view of non-availing of the statutory forum as contended by the respondents.

23. Since the question of maintainability of the instant writ petition has been raised by the respondents' side on the ground of non-exhaustion of the 'equally efficacious forum', this Court is required to deal with the said issue at first.

24. It has been submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the instant writ petition has been filed under both the sub-Articles 1 & 2 of Article 102 of the Constitution.

25. Let us be acquainted with the provisions of Articles 102(1) & 102(2) of our Constitution which are reproduced herein below:

Article 102. Powers of High Court Division to issue certain orders and directions. etc.(I) The High Court Division on the application of any person aggrieved, may give such directions or orders to any person or authority, including any person performing any function in connection with the affairs of the Republic, as may be appropriate for the enforcement of any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of this Constitution .

(2) the High Court Division may, if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided by law-

(a) on the application of any person aggrieved, make an order-

(i) directing a person performing any functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local . authority to refrain from doing that which he is not permitted by law to do or to do that which he is required by law to do; or

(ii) declaring that any act done or proceeding taken by a person performing functions in connection with the affairs of the Republic or of a local authority and is of no legal effect; or

(b) on the application of any person, make an order-

(i) directing that a person in custody be brought before it so that it may satisfy itself that he is not being held in custody without lawful authority or in an unlawful manner; or

(ii) requiring person holding or purporting to hold a public office to show under ,what authority he claims to hold that office.

26. It appears that the jurisdiction of this Court under Articles 102(1) and Article 102(2) is the 'Special Original Jurisdiction' and both the sub-Articles confer an extraordinary power upon the High Court Division and this power should be exercised on its discretion inasmuch as in both the sub-Articles the word "may" has been employed with the following phraseology "may give such direction or orders" in Article 102(1) and "may make an order" in Article 102(2).

<u>27. The fundamental difference between these two sub-Articles is that while Article 102(1) can be invoked directly if an aggrieved person can make out a case of infringement of fundamental rights, however, in order to qualify to be an applicant under Article 102(2), the aggrieved person must satisfy the Court that 'there is no other equally efficacious remedy' to redress his grievance.</u>

28. Now, the pertinent question comes for consideration by this Court as to whether the grievance of the petitioner does fall within the purview of Article 102(1) of the Constitution as has been submitted by the petitioner's side that the impugned decision has been taken in sheer violation of Articles 27, 31 and 40 of the Constitution.

<u>29. However, in our way of scrutiny; we do not find any elements of violation of the above fundamental rights inasmuch as in order to be in a competent position to allege violation of Article. 27 the petitioner is required to establish the fact that she was at par with respondent No.5 but the petitioner's offer being found to be different from that of respondent No.5, Article 27 of the Constitution has hardly any scope to rescue her. Article 31 also cannot be resorted to by the petitioner inasmuch as there must be a clear case of not treating the petitioner as per law inasmuch as there may be violation of law by the respondents in dealing with the petitioner's matter but it is not capable of attracting Article 31 of the Constitution, for instances, (i) when a worker is not treated by his employer, he is to seek redress in the Labour Court, (ii) when a person's property is refused illegally to be mutated by the Assistant Commissioner of land; he is to appeal before the ADC, (iii) when a government servant is declined to enjoy his service benefits, he is to approach Administrative Tribunal and so on. In all the above instances, there are always allegations of not treating the aggrieved party in accordance with law but it cannot be said that there has been violation of Article 31. Finally, Article 40 being a qualified right its violation can 'be agitated only when an aggrieved person shall make out a successful case that despite the fact that the law, by which one's profession or business is to be dealt with, has declared a right to enjoy something but due to the authority's particular action, omission, decision or order she has been deprived of the same, which is not the case here. In dealing with the complaints by the litigants as to their violation of fundamental rights, this Division should be mindful as to whether the said allegation does at all come within the coverage of fundamental rights as has been observed by his Lordship MH Rahman J, as he then was, in the celebrated case of Mujibur Rahman vs Bangladesh 44 DLR (AD) 111 (relevant para 49) that</u>

<u>"An aggrieved person may, out of desperation or just for taking a sportive chance in the summary writ jurisdiction, allege contravention of some fundamental right which may turn out to be frivolous or vexatious or not even remotely attracted in his case. The Court is, however, to be on guard so that the great value of the right given under Article 102(1) is not frittered away or misused as a substitute for more appropriate remedy available for an unlawful action involving no infringement of any fundamental right".</u>

30. The petitioner's grievance, thus, does not come within the periphery of Article 102(1) of our Constitution.

31. The aforesaid conclusion leads us to undertake the examination as to whether the petitioner's grievance is amenable under Article 102(2) of our Constitution.

<u>32. Jurisdiction under Article 102(2), as a whole, is known as an extraordinary jurisdiction and the same is to be availed of only when there is 'no other equally efficacious remedy' available. The framers of the Constitution have intended that the people, at first, must search for and approach an appropriate legal forum other than the Constitutional Court. It is only then the Constitutional Court should be availed of when the citizen will find that the state has not created any legal forum for them for vindication of their right and getting the desired remedy. Thereafter, subject to the 'satisfaction' of this Court, a writ petition may be entertained. Article 102(2) of our Constitution may be quoted in this context. 'The High Court Division if satisfied that no other equally efficacious remedy is provided in law ..........’ It appears from the words employed in the said Article that 'if satisfied' strongly suggests that this 'Special original jurisdiction' of the High Court Division may be invoked only upon the satisfaction of the High Court Division as to the non- availability of the 'other equally efficacious remedy' (underlined for emphasize), In our opinion, the clear and unambiguous words of our Constitution 'if satisfied' mandates this Court to undertake the scrutiny as to the competency of invoking this 'Special original jurisdiction' before issuance of any Rule given that carrying out of the examination thereto after issuance of a Rule may cause sufferings for the parties of the case in addition to wasting valuable time of this Court ill the event of discharging the Rule on this ground.</u>

33. In order to be satisfied as to the availability of the 'equally efficacious remedy' this Court is required to be acquainted with the provisions of the jurisdiction and power of the forum created by the statute namely the PPA, 2006 and the Rules thereunder namely, the PPR, 2008.

34. Here, in the case at hand, respondent Nos. 1-3 invited tender for procurement of some goods for the state and the regulating law for purchasing goods/service for the state is Public Procurement Act, 2006 and the Public Procurement Rules, 2008. Sections 29 and 30 provide the rights and forums for agitating any grievance in connection with any public procurement, which run as follows:

২৯। অভিযোগ করিবার অধিকার।-(১) কোন ব্যক্তি এই আইনের অধীন ক্রয়কারীর উপর অর্পিত দায়িত্ব পালনে ব্যর্থতার জন্য ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হইলে বা তাহার ক্ষতিগ্রস্ত হইবার সম্ভাবনা থাকিলে তিনি উক্ত ক্রয়কারীর বিরুদ্ধে ধারা ৩০ এ বর্ণিত কর্তৃপক্ষে নিকট অভিযোগ দায়ের করিতে পারিবেন।

��০। প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট অভিযোগ দায়ের, আপীল, ইত্যাদি।-(১) ধারা ২৯ এর অধীন দায়েরতব্য প্রতিটি অভিযোগ সংশ্লিষ্ট ক্রয়কারীর প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট দায়ের করিতে হইবে এবং উক্তরুপে কোন অভিযোগ দায়ের হইলে, উক্ত কর্তৃপক্ষ উহা বিবেচনাক্রমে নির্ধারিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে উহা নিষ্পত্তি করিবে।

(২) কোন ব্যক্তি, যদি প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃক প্রদত্ত সন্তুষ্ট না হন বা উক্ত কর্তৃপক্ষ যথাসময়ে সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিতে ব্যর্থ হয়, তাহা হইলে সংক্ষুদ্ধ ব্যক্তি সেই ক্ষেত্রে সরকার বা তৎকর্তৃক নির্ধারিত কোন কর্তৃপক্ষের মাধ্যমে রিভিউ প্যানেলের নিকট আপীল করিতে পারিবেন।

35. From a minute reading of the above pro- visions of law, it is apparent that any person (কোন ব্যক্তি) may lodge a complaint to the concerned administrative authority (প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষ) under section 30(1) in two circumstances namely (1) where he suffers loss due to the failure of the procuring entity in performing its duty or (2) where he (any person) apprehends that there is a likelihood of suffering loss. In the event of dissatisfaction with the decision of the above-mentioned authority, s/he may prefer an appeal to the Review Panel.

36. The petitioner's grievance is that she has suffered loss for the failure of the respondents in performing their duties inasmuch as when the petitioner being a technically responsive bidder was expecting to have the award of the tender as the lowest bidder, she was declared financially non-responsive and, in the said premises, though she is required to approach the forums under section 30 of the PPA, 2006, however, the apparent reasons, as contended by the petitioner, for non-availing the forum under the said section 30 of the PPA, 2006 are that her position falls within the ambit of section ২৯ (২) (গ) (আ) of the PPA, 2006 and, as such, she is debarred from invoking the provisions of Section ২৯(১) of the PPA, 2006. Let us look at the said provisions of the PPA, 2006, which are as under:

২৯(২) নিম্নবর্ণিত ক্ষেত্রে উপ-ধারা (১) এর অধীন কোন অভিযোগ দায়ের করা যাইবে না যথাঃ-

(ক) পণ্য, কার্য বা সেবা ক্রয় পদ্ধতি নির্বাচন;

(খ) কোন আবেদনকারীর সংক্ষিপ্ত তালিকাভুক্তির আবেদন প্রত্যাখ্যান;

(গ) যে সকল ক্ষেত্রে নিম্নবর্ণিত সিদ্ধান্ত হইয়াছে-

(অ) প্রাক-যোগ্যতার আবেদন, দরপত্র, কোটেশন বা প্রস্তাব বাতিল করিবার সিদ্ধান্ত; বা

(আ) সরকারী ক্রয় সংক্রান্ত মন্ত্রিসভা কমিটি কর্তৃক অনুমোদনের পরিপ্রেক্ষিতে চুক্তি সম্পাদনের সিদ্ধান্ত।

37. From a close reading of the above provisions of section ২৯(১) it appears that there are exceptional circumstances where the right to agitate grievance in a public procurement matter under section ২৯(২) of the PPA has been made inapplicable. It is the petitioner's plea that since the Cabinet Committee on Public. Procurement headed by the Hon'ble Prime Minister has already given approval to the decision of the TEC, the forum for agitating her grievance as to declaring her financially a non-responsive bidder is not available to her.

38. Now let us examine the petitioner's plea in the laboratory of law. We find from the reading of section ২৯(১) of the PPA, 2006 that forum under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 becomes available not only when a person suffers loss by the decision of the purchasing entity, but also when a person foresees the probability of suffering loss by the action/omission or decision of the purchasing entity. From the letter dated 27-12-2012 (annexure-i) it appears that the petitioner had approached the administrative authority (প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষ) of the purchasing entity well before the matter got approval of the Cabinet Committee on Public Procurement as she somehow had come to know that she was likely to be prejudiced by the decision of the purchasing entity when the latter replied to the former on 3-1-2013 informing that she had been found financially non-responsive. Thus, we find that after receiving the decision from the administrative authority under Rule 57(7) of the PPR, 2008, the petitioner .had the opportunity to approach the Review Panel under section 30(2) of the PPA, 2006 but she opted not to exhaust the aforesaid forum of Review' Panel.

39. The other reason, as stated by the petitioner, for not approaching the forums under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 is that since the petitioner at no point in time had received a decision on her tender application, she was not in a position to invoke the said forums under section 30 of the PPA, 2006. However, as it has already been found from the petitioner's aforesaid letter dated 27-12- 2012 (annexure i) that she has, in fact, invoked Section 30(1) of the PPA, 2006 by approaching the administrative authority (প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষ) of the purchasing entity, the fact does not require detailed examination.

40. However, having skimmed through the petitioner's letter dated 27-12-2012 submitted to the Secretary, Ministry of Power & Electricity any one with ordinary prudence is led to take a view that since the tender in question is an open tender, apparently the contentions of the said letter come under the provisions of Rule 56(b)(9) & (11) of the PPR, 2008, which run as follows:

41. Thereafter, vide annexure 7 dated 3-1- 2013 the administrative authority (প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষ) communicated its decision to the petitioner informing that she is found financially non-responsive. It has been alleged by the petitioner that she has never received the said decision dated 3-1-2013. The resolution of this issue of receiving or non-receiving the said communication dated 3- 1-2013 being a disputed question of fact, this Court requires the examination of witnesses as to who dispatched the letter and who received the same, exercise of which is normally declined by this Court except in a rare of the rarest cases. On this count as well, the present writ petition may be declared to be not maintainable. However, if the contention of the petitioner as to non-receiving of the respondents' decision is accepted, even then she could have availed the forum under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 in view of the provisions laid down in Rule 57(9) of the PPR, 2008 with the following wordings

৫৭। (৯) কোন ব্যক্তি প্রত্যেকটি স্তরের জন্য নির্ধারিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে লিখিত সিদ্ধান্ত প্রাপ্ত না হইলে, উক্ত ব্যক্তি তফসিল-২ এ বর্ণিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে সরাসরি উক্ত কর্তৃপক্ষের পরবর্তী উর্ধ্বতন কর্তৃপক্ষের নিকট আপীল করিতে পারিবে।

42. On the other hand, from the legal point of view, the petitioner's above plea of non-receiving a decision on her tender application does not appear as a barrier in seeking redress from the authority under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 in view of the provisions of section 29(1) in the following words “ক্ষতিগ্রস্থ হইবার সম্ভাবনা থাকিলে” Thus, it appears that even if the contentions of the petitioner are accepted that she was not given any decision by the purchasing entity, it does not refrain the petitioner from lodging a complaint to the administrative authority (প্রশাসনিক কর্তৃপক্ষ) at first if she feels that she is likely to suffer loss by the action or decision of the purchasing entity and, then, in the event of her non-satisfaction with the decision of the administrative authority she may prefer an appeal to the Review Panel.

<u>43. Furthermore, in an open tender under Rule 56(11) of the PPR, 2008 (“দূর্নীতি বা চক্রান্তমূলক কার্যকলাপ সম্পর্কে সন্দেহ হইলে”) if there is any suspicion of any malafide activities in the process of any public procurement and under Rule 56(12) of the PPR, 2008 (“ক্রটিপূর্ণ বা অন্যায়ভাবে চুক্তি সম্পাদন করা হইয়াছে বলিয়া ধারনা করিবার সঙ্গত কারন থাকিলে”) if there is reason to believe that the contract has been sealed unfairly, anyone can take recourse to section 29 and 30 of the PPA, 2006.</u>

<u>44. From a plain reading of sections 29 & 30 in tandem with Rule 56(b )(9) and 57(9) of the PPR, 2008, it is our considered view that in an open tender if the Tender Evaluation Committee fails to perform its duty in accordance with the provisions of the PPA, 2006, PPR, 2008 and instruction stipulated in the Tender Document, then, anyone who suffers loss or is likely to suffer loss can lodge a complaint against the purchaser to the administrative authority at first and, then, to Review panel if aggrieved by the administrative authority's decision.</u>

45. In the backdrop of the above findings by this Court that there is a specific forum in a special law, now we may proceed to see the powers of the said forum as enumerated in Rule 59 and 60 of the PPR, 2008, which are as under:

৫৯। আপীলের নিম্পত্তি না হওয়া পর্যন্ত চুক্তি সম্পাদনের নোটিশ জারী করা হইতে বিরত থাকর জন্য নির্দেশ প্রদানের ক্ষমতা।-(১) সিপিটিইউ, তফসিল-২ এ উল্লিখিত নির্ধারিত নিবন্ধন ফী এবং নিরাপত্তা জামানতসহ কোন আপীল আবেদন প্রাপ্তির পর, তফসিল-২ এ বর্ণিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে, পালাক্রমে একটি রিভিউ প্যানেল নির্বাচন করিয়া উহার নিকট উক্ত আপীল আবেদন নিম্পত্তির জন্য প্রেরণ করিবে এবং উক্ত বিষয়ে রিভিউ প্যানেলের সিদ্ধান্ত না পাওয়া পর্যন্ত রিভিউ প্যানেল এর বিবেচনাধীন কোন ক্রয়কার্য বিষয়ে চু্িকত সম্পাদন করা হইতে বিরত থাকার জন্য ক্রয়কারীকে নির্দেশ প্রদান করিয়া সংশ্লিষ্ট মন্ত্রণালয় বা বিভাগের সচিব ও আবেদনকারীকে গৃহীত ব্যবস্থা সম্পর্কে পত্র মারফত অবহিত করিবে।

(২) ক্রয়কারী বা রিভিউ প্যানেলের নিকট কোন অভিযোগ বা আপীল বিবেচনাধীন থাকিলে উক্ত অভিযোগ বা আপীলের উপর চুড়ান্ত সিদ্ধান্ত না হওয়া পর্যন্ত চুক্তি সম্পাদনের নোটিশ জারী করা যাইবে না, তবে অভিযোগ বিবেচনাধীন থাকাকালীন দরপত্র মূল্যায়ন ও উহার অনুমোদন প্রক্রিয়া অব্যাহত রাখা যাইবে।

৬০। রিভিউ প্যানেল কর্তৃক আপীল নিষ্পত্তি।-(১) কোন আপীল আবেদন রিভিউ প্যানেলের সিদ্ধান্তের জন্য প্রেরণ করা হইলে এবং উক্ত আপীল যথাযথ নিরাপত্তা জামানত ও নিবন্ধন ফিসসহ দায়েরকৃত হইলে রিভিউ প্যানেল, উহার সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদানের সময় পর্যন্ত, চুক্তি সম্পাদনের নোটিশ জারী সংক্রান্ত স্থগিতদেশ অব্যাহত রাখিতে ক্রয়কারীকে পরামর্শ দিবে।

(২) রিভিউ প্যানেল, তফসিল-২এ বর্ণিত সময়সীমার মধ্যে উহার লিখিত সিদ্ধান্ত প্রদান করিবে এবং উক্ত সিদ্ধান্তের কপি সংশ্লিষ্ট ব্যক্তি, সংশ্লিষ্ট মন্ত্রণালয় বা বিভাগের সচিব, সিপিট��ইউ এবং ক্রয়কারীকে প্রদান করিবে।

<u>46. From a plain reading of the Rules 59 & 60, it appears that the forum created by the statute namely PPA, 2006 under section 30 of the same is amply empowered to adjudicate upon any sort of complaint or grievance related to arising out of procurement by a public body with the public money inasmuch as there are abundant provisions for passing interim order restraining the purchasing entity from entering into the contract until disposal of the complaint or appeal.</u>

47. In order to know as to what types of power the Review Panel possesses or what kind of order it can pass and whether the decision of the Review Panel has the binding effect on the public authorities, let us look at Rules 60(3) & 60(5) of the PPR, 2008, which run as follows:

৬০(৩) তুচ্ছ (frivolous) কারণে অভিযোগ দায়েরের কারণে উহা খারিজ এবং ক্ষেত্রমত, নিরাপত্তা জামানত বাজেয়াপ্ত করার ক্ষেত্রে ব্যতীত, আপীল নিষ্পত্তির ক্ষেত্রে, রিভিউ প্যানেল নিম্নবর্ণিত যে কোন সিদ্ধান্ত স্বতন্ত্রভাবে বা সম্মিলিতভাবে প্রদান করিতে পারিবে, যথাঃ

<u>48.	Under the provisions of Rule 60 (3) of the PPR, 2008 the Review Panel is empowered to pass any kind of order as it deems appropriate including payment of costs and compensation and Rule 60 (5) of the PPR, 2008 makes the decision of the Review Panel to be the final verdict and the same is binding upon the purchasing entity. In the case of BTCL vs CPTU, 18 BLC 98 it was held that "the decision of the Review Panel, be that advice, recommendation or direction, will be binding upon all the parties (Para-17)". Moreover, section 4 of the PPA, 2006 heralds that it is a special law having overriding effect on other laws and the Review Panel being constituted with 3 (three) highly knowledgeable adjudicators, one having experience from the field of administration, one from judiciary and the third one from technical field of relevant procuring staff, the forum appears to be one of the most competent and best forum any statute has ever created in our country for speedy and complete disposal of this kind of complicated grievances. The above discussions on the power and jurisdiction of the Review Panel leads us to conclude that the forum under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 is a 'better forum' than an "equally efficacious" forum for adjudication of the petitioner's grievance as it has the power to stay the further proceedings of the procurement process and, then, to dispose of the complaint and, thereafter, to finally adjudicate upon the appeal within the stipulated time as fixed in the 'schedule 2' of the Rule with or without costs and, if appropriate, to compensate the aggrieved party. Accordingly, on the basis of the above discussions, we hold that the instant writ petition does not come within the ambit of Article 102 (2) of the Constitution.</u>

49. We should now deal with the submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that even if there is an alternative remedy the instant writ petition is maintainable as the impugned decision is taken without jurisdiction and, also, the same is tainted with malafide action. We, in dealing with the above submissions, are required to succinctly delve into the case laws referred to by the petitioner.

50. Let us, first, briefly examine the facts as well as law under which the cited case laws were adjudicated upon in order to see as to whether their ratio decidendi are applicable in the present case.

51. The case of Abdur Rouf and vs Abdul Hamid Khan reported in 17 DLR (SC) 515 was regarding a dispute over land properties, which was sent to the Deputy Commissioner as a reference under a Regulation (Frontier Criminal Regulation) for adjudicating of the matter and, as per sections 10 and 60 of the said Regulation, the order of the Deputy Commissioner was final. Then, question arose as to whether the dispute was at all referable to the Deputy Commissioner and it was found by the Supreme Court that the matter was sent as a reference to the DC under misconception of law and, therefore, the order passed by the DC was without jurisdiction. The facts of the above-cited case and the law points involved therein being different from that of the instant case, its dictum is not applicable here.

52. In the case of Begum Lutfunnessa vs Bangladesh 42 DLR (AD) 86 the writ petitioner's grievance was that her property was included in the list of abandoned property though she was in physical possession of the same and when the High Court Division rejected the writ petition on the ground that there was an alternative remedy under section 7 of the Abandoned Building Ordinance, 1985, the Apex Court held that the writ petition is maintainable given that when the writ petitioner filed the writ petition on 19-8-1986 challenging the publication of the impugned list under notice dated 28-4-1986, there was no Settlement Court in operation under section 7 and, further, the Apex Court found that since the fact of possessing the property by the writ petitioner was not denied by the respondents, inclusion of the writ petitioner's property in the list of abandoned property was ex facie without jurisdiction. Thus, it appears that the facts and legal issues of the cited case is completely different from the fact of the case at hand and, this, the ratio decidendi of the said case law is not applicable in this case.

53. In the case of Nesar Ahmed vs Bangladesh 49 DLR (AD) 111 the writ petitioner challenged the judgment and order passed by the Special Tribunal convicting him for 10 years in prison when the High Court Division rejected the writ petition in limine on the ground that there is an alternative remedy of appeal under section 30 of the Special Powers Act, 1974. However, the Appellate Division held that as the appellant had no reasonable opportunity to face the trial and, thereafter, to avail of the alternative remedy his writ petition was maintainable and, in addition thereto, it was also found that the recovered torch light and rope being not arms within the provisions of the Arms Act, the trial and conviction was without jurisdiction. But in the case at hand, the petitioner had the opportunity to avail the alternative forum and the decision of the respondents having attracted the mischief of some provisions of the PPA, 2006 and PPR, 2008 cannot be said to have been made without jurisdiction.

54. The case of Government of Bangladesh vs Sayeda Chand Sultana 51 DLR (AD) 24 was with regard to challenging the inclusion of the petitioner's property in the list of abandoned property though he was in possession thereof during and after the liberation war and the aforesaid fact was not rebutted by the government and, in that premise, the. High Court Division as well as the Appellate Division held that the impugned decision was without jurisdiction.

55. The above four case laws were referred to by the petitioner in a bid to show that the impugned decision was taken by the respondents without jurisdiction and, hence, the instant writ petition is maintainable without availing the forum under section 30 of the PPA, 2006. However, since the discussions made herein before suggest that the facts of the afore-cited cases being different from that of the present case and the principles laid down in the above cases, are not relevant at all to this case and, as such, it cannot be applied here inasmuch as our jurisprudence on the word "without jurisdiction" has subsequently developed in clear terms making the word applicable in specific situation/case.

<u>56. The fact of the cases of (i) Hyundai Corporation vs Sumikin Bussan Corporation 54 DLR (AD) 88 and (ii) Ekushey Television vs Chowdhury Mahmud Hassan 54 DLR (AD) 130 (Popularly Known as ETV case) appear to be almost similar to the present case. In both of the cases the actions of the government authorities were found to have been taken aiming at favouring their chosen persons and in entertaining the writ petitions, which was affirmed by the Appellate Division, our Courts heavily relied upon the dictum propounded in the case of Tata Cellular vs Union of India AIR 1996 (SC) 11. However, at that point in time the PPA, 2006 was not in place and, therefore, there was no equally efficacious forum functioning under section 30 of the PPA, 2006 to take recourse to redress any grievance related to public procurement. Thus, the ratio decidendi of these two cases have lost their force so far as it relates to the issue of maintain- ability of a writ petition on the grievance of public procurement after the enactment of the PPA, 2006 and, as such, the same is not applicable in the case at hand.</u>

57. Much reliance was placed by both the parties on the issue as to whether the contract is a statutory contract upon referring to the celebrated case of Sharping MSS 39 DLR (AD) 85 and Superintendent Engineer, RHD vs Md Eunus and Brothers (Pvt) Ltd 31 BLD (AD) 1. However, the dictum of these two cases or such like others cases are not applicable in the grievance related to the purchasing of public services/goods with the public money given that appropriate provisions have now been incorporated in the PPA, 2006 for dealing with statutory contracts.

58. To substantiate his argument that the impugned decision is an offspring of malafide, the case, of (i) Khandaker Mostaque Ahmed vs Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 223, (ii) Jamil Huq vs Bangladesh reported in 34 DLR (AD) 125 and (iii) Kh. Ehteshamuddin Ahmed vs Bangladesh reported in 33 DLR (AD) 154 were cited before this Court. In all these three cases writ petitions were filed challenging the convictions passed by the Tribunal set up under the Martial Law Ordinance (MLO). Schedule of the said MLO incorporated provision for this Court to review actions and proceedings of the Tribunals and, therefore, there was scope in the said MLO itself to review the actions of the Martial Law Tribunals. When the issue of maintainability of these writ petitions were raised on the ground of operation of the ouster provisions under Article 102(5) of our Constitution, it was observed by our Apex Court that the High Court's jurisdiction under Article 102 may be exercised if the authority of a disciplined force or Courts/Tribunal under the Army Act or other law relating to disciplined forces acts malafide or without jurisdiction or is not properly constituted. It is to be noted here that though all the aforesaid three cases laid down the above principle of invoking writ jurisdiction over-riding the exception of Article 102(5) of the Constitution, but, interestingly enough, in all of the cases, writ petitions were rejected summarily, which were upheld by the Appellate Division. The ratio decidendi of the above cases are not applicable in the instant case inasmuch as the petitioners of the afore cited cases did not jump directly to the High Court Division when they were accused of committing the offence under Army Act bypassing the Tribunal. Here in this case, the petitioner approached the High Court Division straightaway without submitting herself to the Review Panel. Also, from the facts of the above cases and the conclusion arrived at by the Apex Court therein, it is our view that the aforesaid principle seems to be applicable only to the criminal cases.

<u>59. Mala fide connotes malice in fact; meaning that when a public authority acts maliciously affecting adversely the right of a citizen, the said authority is blamed to have acted malafide. In order to successfully make out a case on the basis of malafide, the petitioner is required to categorically state the grudge against her, if any, or to produce the proof/evidence of naked favour by the respondents to another party. Allegations of malafide on vague or general terms is beyond the scope of consideration by this Court. Here in this case the decision of the respondents in declaring the petitioner financially non-responsive has been branded to be malafide on the ground that the respondents have purposefully excluded the name of the petitioner from the list of the financially responsive bidders because they had an ulterior motive to favour respondent No.5 in awarding the contract and, in a bid to substantiate this allegation, the petitioner has relied upon mainly on the following facts (i) she is the lowest bidder with a margin of 200 crores Taka, (ii) the grounds taken for rejection of her bid are not related with financial part, rather technical part and (iii) she has not been provided with a copy of the decision as to finding her non-responsive. However, out of the above facts while last two have been denied completely by the respondents, the first one has been disputed in other way round stating that until a bidder is found to be responsive there is no scope to compare the rate of any bidder. Thus, the allegations raised by the petitioner appear to be disputed questions of fact and the same are beyond the adjudication of this Court.</u>

60. In our assessment, the foregoing assertion that until the petitioner is found to be responsive both technically and financially there is hardly any scope to consider the rate apparently may sound to be acceptable but its adjudication being interrelated with the allegation No.2, both the allegation Nos. 1 & 2 should be dealt with analogously. With regard to the third allegation that annexure-I and annexure-7 were never communicated to the petitioner and he was not informed about the decision of the TEC, the concerned person of the respondents is required to corroborate the same by adducing his/her evidence for which the petitioner may approach the Review Panel.

<u>61. Our above view should not be misunderstood to be a conservative stand as we are not curtailing the power of the High Court Division nor this judgment is aimed at reduction of the number of briefs of the members of this Bar. This Court in past has never hesitated or shall not be shaky in future to entertain writ petitions in fit and proper cases, for example, where an action taken or order passed by a Government or any statutory body or even any Constitutional body is ex facie illegal, malafide, or the same suffers from malice-in-law or quorum non-judice in carrying out its functions within administrative capacity, inspite of the existence of other alternative forums.</u>

62. Before we part with the judgment, this Court feels it pertinent to overview on the tasks of the Review Panel. Here it is pertinent to refer to the facts and dictum of the case of RAJUK vs Abdur Raul Chowdhury 61 DLR (AD) 28 where the writ petitioner Mr. Abdur Rouf Chowdhury constructed a 22 storied building near the Tejgaon Airport and RAJUK alleged that the same has been done without obtaining any planning per- mission from them and, eventually, it threatened to dismantle the building when the High Court Division though made the Rule absolute but on an appeal the Apex Court ordered for demolishing the building. The purpose of referring this case here is that the Court can pass an order to demolish a project if it is required for protection of the national interest. However, in this case there should not be any order to demolish the project for the protection of financial interest of the state. In the cited case, the order of demolition was passed in order to protect the interest of the state i.e. to protect the Tejgaon Airport and, here the national interest is installation of the project with the minimum cost and maxim quality. Thus, if it is required in this case any appropriate order may be passed by the Review Panel without hampering the ongoing construction and installation work of the project upon unhesitatingly detecting the illegality and lack of transparency, if there is any, towards adjudication of this sensitive public procurement related complaint.

72. In our jurisdiction the power of judicial review of this Court flows from the mandate of Article 102 of our Constitution unlike the UK where inspite of not having any written legal man- date, their judiciary exercises this power. However, the British judiciary since long has formulated some rules, principles/guidelines as to where the judicial power should be exercised. Among them, one rule is constantly being followed by them that if there is any forum created by any law, the UK judiciary does not entertain the judicial review application.

73. In our jurisdiction as well, our Apex Court has repeatedly reminded the High Court Division to be skeptical in entertaining writ petition where there is an alternative forum. In a series of decisions our Apex Court disapproved invocation of writ jurisdiction by circumventing the alternative forum. In a recent case, ACC vs Enayetur Rahman, 64 DLR (AD) 14, when the ACC filed charge-sheet against the petitioner he invoked the writ jurisdiction for quashing the criminal proceedings and the High Court Division quashed the proceeding but the Appellate Division set-aside the verdict on the ground that the High Court Division should not have entertained the writ petition when there is an alternative forum.
